title: Armorican terranes split from Gondwana

facts.text: The Armorican Terrane Assemblage split away from Gondwana in the Silurian and drifted toward Laurussia through the Devonian.
Its complete separation, across the young Paleo-Tethys, is thought to have come toward the end of the Silurian.
Armorica later collided with Laurussia in the Variscan orogeny, late in the Carboniferous.

title: Armoured jawless fish radiate

facts.text: By the Late Silurian the armoured jawless fish (ostracoderms) reached the high point of their evolution.
Anaspids appear in the early Silurian; osteostracans, probably arising in Euramerica, appear in the Llandovery or Wenlock.
Thelodont scales were widespread worldwide; the tadpole-like archipelepidiforms, basal thelodonts, lived from the late Telychian to the Sheinwoodian.
Heterostracans of the order Traquairaspidiformes appear in the Late Silurian.
The Silurian rise of jawed fish coincided with a sharp decline of jawless fish such as conodonts and ostracoderms.

title: Asaphid trilobites die out

facts.text: Asaphida, a large and varied trilobite order known since the Middle Cambrian, died out during the Silurian.
Its last members, the Trinucleioidea, disappeared before the end of the period.

title: Clinton ironstones laid down in Appalachian basin

facts.text: Shale, mudstone, sandstone and iron-rich 'Clinton Ironstones' of the Clinton Group built up in the Appalachian Foreland Basin, from New York to Alabama, in the early Silurian.
Richly fossiliferous, the Clinton Group is an important record of early Silurian marine life.
It is best known as a significant source of iron ore.

title: Jawed fish diversify

facts.text: A major Silurian milestone was the diversification of jawed fish: placoderms, acanthodians and bony fish.
Cartilaginous and bony fish, the jawed groups still alive today, appeared by the late Silurian.
Fish diversified greatly in the Silurian and Devonian, though with fewer new body plans than in the Cambrian explosion.
Lobe-finned fish (Sarcopterygii) emerged in the Silurian and early Devonian, all still aquatic.
By about 419 Ma jawed fish had split into placoderms, bony fish and the spiny-shark/cartilaginous-fish clade; the placoderm Entelognathus already had a bony jaw skeleton.

facts.text: Most stromatoporoid sponge orders, including Amphiporida and Stromatoporida, originated in the Silurian.

title: Nematophytes tower over early land plants

facts.text: Nematophytes, a loose group of land organisms including some plants and algae, are known from the Silurian to the Early Devonian.
They towered over even the largest land plants and formed networks of large, mycorrhizal forms; truly larger plants came only in the Early Carboniferous.
Nematothallus is first recorded in the Ludfordian, alongside Cooksonia in Ludlow rocks.

title: Rheic Ocean at its widest

facts.text: As Avalonia–Carolina drifted north from Gondwana, the Rheic Ocean reached its greatest width, about 4,000 km, in the Silurian.
It separated Laurussia to the north from Gondwana to the south.

title: Silurian base defined at Dob's Linn

facts.text: Dob's Linn, a small valley in southern Scotland, holds the reference section (GSSP) for the Ordovician–Silurian boundary and the base of the Llandovery.
The boundary is set where the graptolites Parakidograptus acuminatus and Akidograptus ascensus first appear in the Birkhill Shale.
The base of the Silurian follows the end-Ordovician extinctions, which wiped out up to 60% of marine genera.

title: Marine life rebounds after end-Ordovician extinction

facts.text: As melting ice raised sea level and re-flooded continental shelves, biodiversity rebounded within the surviving orders.
Early Silurian communities were simpler and broader-niched, but faunas became among the most cosmopolitan of the Phanerozoic.
Many 'Lazarus taxa' missing from the latest Ordovician reappeared, so small populations had survived in refuges.
Atrypid brachiopods and trilobites began recovering in the Rhuddanian; pentamerid brachiopods not until the Aeronian.
Sponges dominated South China's oxygen-poor seafloors in the earliest Rhuddanian; bryozoans and echinoderms soon recovered too.

title: First placoderms appear

facts.text: The first identifiable placoderms, armoured jawed fish, appear in the late Llandovery.
The vertebrate jaw probably evolved in the Silurian and appeared in placoderms, which diversified further in the Devonian.
Their Silurian record is fragmentary, probably because they lived where fossils rarely formed; the antiarch Silurolepis from Ludlow rocks of Yunnan is a rare near-complete find.

title: Land plants spread widely

facts.text: Mercury isotope excursions show land plants had spread across much of Earth's land surface by the Early Silurian.
Plants were already moving onto land in the Llandovery; Eohostimella, probably a land plant, is known from rocks about 440–430 Ma.
Spores and plant microfossils of this age have been found in China and Pennsylvania.
Silurian land floras were broadly similar across the globe, with little regional difference.

title: Reef building expands

facts.text: Widespread reef building began in the Llandovery and continued into the Devonian.
Barrier reefs covered much more seafloor than reefs do today and grew even at high latitudes; tabulate corals formed prominent mounds.
Coral photosymbiosis may have begun in the Llandovery; photosymbiotic corals appear by the Middle Silurian.
Hederelloids flourished, some living in symbiosis with the rugose coral Entelophyllum.

facts.text: The Taconic orogeny, which built mountains across New England, ended about 440 Ma.
Subduction stopped and the Iapetus Terrane was accreted onto eastern North America.
As the mountains eroded in the Silurian and Devonian, sediment spread over the Appalachians and the North American midcontinent.

title: Silurian glaciations centred on South America

facts.text: Milder glaciations followed the Hirnantian ice age through the Silurian, the last in the Late Silurian.
The centre of glaciation moved from the Sahara to South America; ice is recorded in Arabia, West Africa, the Amazon and the Andes.
Glacial phases struck in the early and latest Aeronian, late Telychian to mid-Sheinwoodian, Homerian and Ludfordian.
Silurian ice caps were smaller than the Late Ordovician ones, and glaciers almost vanished by mid-Silurian.
A lack of tillites in the middle to late Silurian makes glaciation a problematic explanation for its climate swings.
Qianodus and Fanjingshania, from Aeronian rocks in Guizhou, China, about 439 Ma, are the oldest unambiguous remains of jawed vertebrates.
Both are acanthodian-grade stem chondrichthyans, early relatives of cartilaginous fish; possibly older Ordovician records exist.
Acanthodians, the 'spiny sharks', arose about 50 million years before the first true sharks.
Unambiguous jawed-vertebrate fossils, mostly primitive acanthodians, appear by the early Silurian and become abundant by the Devonian.

conflicts.note: Acanthodii page dates the earliest unequivocal acanthodians to the start of the Silurian
Evolution of fish says jawed fish evolved from ostracoderms about 420 Ma

facts.text: The Huixingshao Formation near Chongqing, China, about 436 Ma, preserves complete fossils of the earliest jawed vertebrates.
The site also holds galeaspids and eurypterids.
A fish of this age, Shenacanthus, had placoderm-like armour plates on its chest.
The oldest known bony-fish fossils, about 436 million years old, have teeth arranged midway between those of sharks and true bony fish.
These early bony fish still had mostly cartilaginous skeletons; their novelty was foregut pouches that later became swim bladders and lungs.
Bony fish appeared in the Silurian and became common and diverse in the Devonian.
One of their branches, the lobe-finned fish, later gave rise to all land vertebrates.
Guiyu oneiros, about 425 Ma from Yunnan, China, is one of the earliest articulated bony fish, mixing placoderm-like traits with those of ray- and lobe-finned fish.

title: Scandian phase of the Caledonian orogeny

facts.text: In the Scandian phase of the Caledonian orogeny, Baltica and Laurentia collided from about 435 to 410 Ma.
Avalonia, Baltica and Laurentia drifted together near the equator, starting to form Euramerica.
Mountains rose from New York State through Greenland and Britain to Norway as the collision folded long-accumulated coastal sediments.
Thrusting built Scotland's Moine Thrust Belt (435–420 Ma), and Caledonian nappes stacked up in Scandinavia.
Baltica's margin was buried about 120 km deep around 429 Ma, forming micro-diamonds; trilobite faunas from both sides mixed as the ocean narrowed.

facts.text: Cooksonia, the oldest known vascular plants (tracheophytes), appear in the Wenlock, in the middle of the Silurian.
Cooksonia remained an important part of the flora until the end of the Early Devonian, spanning 433 to 393 Ma.
A Cooksonia species from about 432 Ma, C. barrandei, is known from its spore-bearing stage (sporophyte).
Most Cooksonia-bearing rocks are marine; the plants probably grew along rivers and streams.
Slightly later, more complex Gondwanan plants like Baragwanathia suggest vascular plants have a longer history, perhaps reaching into the early Silurian.

conflicts.note: Timeline of Earth puts the first appearance of Cooksonia at c. 430 Ma

facts.text: The Ireviken event, the first of three Silurian extinctions, struck at the Llandovery–Wenlock boundary and lasted about 200,000 years.
At Ireviken, Gotland, over half of trilobite species died out; worldwide, 80% of conodont species vanished.
It began in the deep ocean and spread to shelf seas: graptolites, conodonts and trilobites suffered most, while shallow reefs were barely touched.
It is linked to global cooling and was followed by a positive carbon isotope excursion (a separate entry).
Its eight extinction steps appear to track orbital (Milankovitch) cycles; sediments of the event show metal enrichment.

title: Isotope excursion after the Ireviken event

facts.text: After the first Ireviken extinctions, δ13C rose from +1.4‰ to +4.5‰ and δ18O from −5.6‰ to −5.0‰.
This early Silurian excursion, about 431 Ma, resembles the Cambrian SPICE event, peaking near +4.5‰.
The Silurian had more isotope excursions, a sign of climate swings, than any other period.

title: Lundgreni event (Mid-Homerian Biotic Crisis)

facts.text: The Lundgreni event, or Mid-Homerian Biotic Crisis, was an extinction in the middle Homerian, recorded in Iberia, Bohemia and Poland.
It hit graptolites, benthic animals and microphytoplankton hardest; graptolite richness hit a global low and cyrtograptids died out.
Eutrophication and anoxia are blamed; a double-peaked positive carbon isotope excursion began with it.

facts.text: Scorpions date back to the Silurian, about 430 Ma; the oldest known, Dolichophonus loudonensis, lived in what is now Scotland.
Whether early scorpions lived in water or on land is debated, though early forms like Eramoscorpius had book lungs.
Land scorpions appear in timelines at about 420 Ma.
The Great Glen Fault formed late in the Caledonian orogeny, as Laurentia and Baltica collided, probably between 430 and 390 Ma.
It shaped the Scottish Highlands.

conflicts.note: Timeline of Earth dates the start of the Great Glen Fault to c. 433 Ma

facts.text: A stepwise mid-Paleozoic rise of oxygen to and above modern levels ran from about 428 to 359 Ma, alongside the spread of vascular plants.
Oxygen stood near 13% of today's level in the early Silurian but approached modern levels in the Devonian.
Land plants' higher photosynthetic yield likely drove it; burying organic carbon in rocks also cut the oxygen sink.
Falling CO2, as carbon was trapped in rocks, also cooled the climate.

conflicts.note: Paleozoic page dates the Paleozoic Oxidation Event 470–400 Ma

facts.text: From 428 to 359 Ma land plants, especially vascular plants, and fungi rapidly colonised and diversified on dry land; the critical phase was the Late Silurian–Early Devonian.
Vascular plants arose from simpler land plants, dikaryan and glomeromycotan fungi spread, and myriapods, arachnids and hexapods became fully terrestrial.
Plant diversity rose on a scale compared with the Cambrian explosion of animals, notably in tall, woody vascular plants that later formed canopies.
Volcanic islands of the Rheic Ocean were hotspots of plant evolution, and the new vegetation reshaped the water cycle and global climate.
It changed ocean nutrients and sediment cycling worldwide, likely feeding plankton blooms tied to the Late Devonian extinction.

conflicts.note: Devonian page: the Devonian Explosion, dated by the period

facts.text: The Mulde event, an anoxic event, was the second of three relatively minor Silurian mass extinctions.
It coincided with a global drop in sea level and was closely followed by an isotope excursion.
Carbon isotopes suggest a sustained drop in CO2 at the time of the extinction.
Its onset matches the Fröjel Formation of Gotland; apparent conodont losses may reflect changed sediments rather than real extinction.
Lycophytes, one of the oldest surviving lineages of vascular plants, date back to the Silurian, about 425 Ma.
Baragwanathia, a clubmoss with branching stems and needle-like leaves 10–20 cm long, was advanced for its age; it is known from Australia, Canada and China.
Middle Silurian plants were mostly under 10 cm tall.
The lycophyte order Drepanophycales ranges from the Late Silurian to the Late Devonian, about 430–360 Ma.

facts.text: Kampecaris obanensis and Archidesmus from Kerrera, Scotland, about 425 Ma, are the definitive oldest millipedes.
Millipedes are among the oldest known land animals and among the first animals to colonise land.
Air-breathing arthropods from Kerrera (425 Ma) and Ludlow (420 Ma) are older than the zircon age of Pneumodesmus.
Land animals had little impact on Earth until they diversified in the Devonian.

facts.text: Palaeoscolecids, worms known since the late Early Cambrian, last appear in the Ludfordian.

title: Ludfordian glaciation and sea-level fall

facts.text: The last major glaciation of the Early Palaeozoic Ice Age struck in the Ludfordian and is associated with the Lau event.
Ice growth in the middle Ludfordian caused a major marine regression, exposing vast new land.
Plants and cyanobacterial mats quickly colonised the new land, furthering plant diversification.

facts.text: The Lau event, last of three Silurian extinctions, began at the start of the late Ludfordian; it is named after Lau parish on Gotland.
It struck conodonts hardest; graptolites suffered in the Kozlowskii event just after, which may have been coeval.
It coincided with a glacially driven global sea-level low, and most major groups saw higher extinction rates.
Rated 6.2 in severity, it permanently altered communities; stromatolites and microbial mats spread, as after the end-Ordovician and end-Permian extinctions.
It may have finished off the palaeoscolecid worms.

facts.text: Eurypterids (sea scorpions) were major parts of Silurian marine faunas, peaking in diversity in the Pridoli, 423 to 419.2 Ma.
Most eurypterid groups are first recorded in Silurian rocks; eurypterines make up 90% of eurypterids in most beds.
Large pterygotids with rudder-like tails and big pincers appeared in the Late Silurian; Acutiramus reached about 2 m.
Eurypterus, the most abundant eurypterid, lived from about 432 Ma to the end of the Pridoli; Pennsylvania's Tonoloway Formation holds a mass assemblage.
The earliest known ascomycete fungi date from 423 to 419 Ma, in the Silurian.
Dikaryan fungi, the group including ascomycetes, began expanding and diversifying in the Silurian.

title: First wildfires

facts.text: Oxygen first rose high enough for wildfires in the Pridoli, when the first charcoal appears in the fossil record.
Silurian charcoal shows oxygen had crossed about 15%, enough to sustain fire for the first time.

title: Šilalė event

facts.text: The Šilalė event, early in the Pridoli, was a conodont extinction marked by a negative carbon isotope excursion.
The isotope low is traced from Lithuanian cores to the Appalachian Basin of North America.
Conodonts declined while brachiopods grew in diversity and abundance; it coincided with the Pridoli's weakest 405,000-year orbital eccentricity cycle.

title: Pneumodesmus, oldest air-breathing land animal

facts.text: Pneumodesmus newmani, a millipede-like myriapod from Scotland, is among the first myriapods and the oldest creatures known to have lived on land.
Openings in its cuticle are read as spiracles, making it the earliest known arthropod with a tracheal system for breathing air.
Its age is disputed: a 2023 study argued for the late Wenlock, about 430 Ma, but zircon dates and a 2025 study favour the Pridoli–Lochkovian, about 414 Ma.
Millipedes, first appearing in the Silurian, are among the oldest known land animals.

contested_note: Its age is disputed: once put at about 428 million years (Wenlock), newer dating suggests closer to 414 million years (Pridoli–Lochkovian).

title: Arachnids and centipedes join millipedes on land

facts.text: By the Pridoli, about 420 Ma, millipedes were joined on land by centipedes and trigonotarbid arachnids.
Timelines list the earliest trigonotarbid arachnids and land scorpions at about 420 Ma.
Predators among them imply simple food webs that included plant- or detritus-eating prey.
Myriapods, arachnids and hexapods all became fully terrestrial during the Silurian–Devonian Terrestrial Revolution.

facts.text: The earliest known ray-finned fish may be Andreolepis hedei, about 420 Ma, found in Russia, Sweden and Estonia.
Timelines list the earliest ray-finned fish at about 420 Ma.
Ray-finned fish now make up the vast majority of living fish; their crown group arose much later, near the Devonian–Carboniferous boundary.
By the end of the Silurian, about 420 Ma, the Iapetus Ocean had closed entirely, leaving the Iapetus Suture.
Avalonia and Baltica fused with Laurentia in the Caledonian orogeny, forming Laurussia, later the northern part of Pangaea.
Laurentia–Avalonia convergence and Iapetus subduction had ceased by about 420 Ma.
Laurussia's southern margin took shape in this collision; peak metamorphism in Scandinavia's thrust sheets came about 420 Ma.

facts.text: Ascocerid cephalopods, cut back by the end-Ordovician extinction, recovered in the Silurian.
They died out abruptly at the end of the Silurian.

title: Late Silurian sea-level fall and Salina evaporites

facts.text: At the end of the Silurian, sea level dropped again, leaving evaporite basins from Michigan to West Virginia; the new mountains eroded rapidly.
A warm, arid late Silurian climate in a shallow inland basin laid down Salina Group evaporites 120–800 m thick.
Sea level had risen through the first half of the Silurian and fell through the rest.
